title: Same Value, Different Risk
problem: Contract A pays $5 for certain. Contract B pays $10 after heads and $0 after tails on a fair coin. Find each fair value and standard deviation. If you must invest your entire $6 bankroll in one contract at its fair price, explain the practical difference.

hints.text: Equal expected values do not imply equal payoff distributions.
For B, compute the average squared deviation of the payoffs 0 and 10 from their mean of 5.

solution.setup: Compare both the mean payoff and the dispersion around that mean.
solution.reasoning: A always pays $5, so its fair value is $5 and standard deviation is 0. B has mean (0+10)/2=$5. Its variance is [(0-5)^2+(10-5)^2]/2=25, so its standard deviation is $5. At a $5 purchase price, both have zero expected profit, but A returns the invested $5 with certainty while B can lose the full $5 stake half the time. With only $6 of capital, that downside can materially constrain future opportunities.
solution.finalAnswer: Both fair values are $5; SD(A)=0 and SD(B)=$5. B carries substantial capital risk despite equal expected value.
solution.sanityCheck: B's payoffs are always exactly $5 away from its mean, so its standard deviation must be $5.

keyInsight: Expected value prices the average payoff, but position decisions also depend on dispersion, downside, and available capital.
recognitionCues: When two choices have similar expected value, inspect the entire payoff distribution and worst-case loss.
commonMistakes: Concluding that equal fair values make the contracts practically interchangeable.
followUps: How would buying many independent copies of B change the risk per dollar of expected payoff?

verification.notes: B has variance 25 from two equiprobable deviations of magnitude 5.
